item.title: What the Lottery Ticket Knows About Addiction
item.description:
Addiction

What the Lottery Ticket Knows About Addiction

Why "it won’t happen to me" may be the most dangerous sentence in the human mind.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • We tend to believe statistics apply to other people, a bias researchers call unrealistic optimism.
  • Immediate rewards can outweigh delayed consequences, especially in addictive behavior.
  • Knowing the odds does not change them, and awareness of risk is not immunity from it.

I once ran into a student at a gas station, buying a lottery ticket. When I asked why, he offered a perfectly constructed explanation: He had an exam the next morning, and it was, he said, statistically impossible to have two pieces of bad luck in one day. Either he would pass the exam, or he would win the lottery. The odds of both failing were simply too low. (The clinical scenes that follow draw on experiences across multiple patients; identifying details and circumstances have been combined and altered.)

He knew plenty about probability—his chance of winning was vanishingly small, and he could recite it. So why spend the money? Perhaps that was the ticket’s real value. It could not meaningfully improve his odds—but it gave him another imaginable route to a good tomorrow. For an anxious mind, that can feel like relief.

He was wrong, of course—chance keeps no ledgers. But he was entirely human. And that brand of wrong is worth taking seriously, because on another night, in another life, it does not cost a few dollars. It costs everything.

The Man Who Had It Under Control

Around the same period, I met a couple, married just over a year, whose marriage was already straining under his drinking. He assured me—with complete sincerity—that he would never become addicted. He had it under control. He exercised almost daily; surely that protected him.

I told him what my clinical work keeps teaching me: I have never met a single person who started drinking, using drugs, or gambling with the intention of becoming addicted. Again and again, patients I have treated for addiction have described some earlier version of the same belief: I can control this. It will not happen to me.

He nodded. He heard me. He did not believe me.

I pointed out that exercise, for all its value, does not make the nervous system immune to alcohol. He was treating good health in one domain as insurance against risk in another, as though fitness earned him a waiver that biology never issues.

The Psychology of "Not Me"

Here is the thread connecting a lottery ticket to the tragedy this post is heading toward: Knowing that a risk exists is psychologically different from experiencing oneself as someone to whom the risk can happen. Several distinct mechanisms feed that gap; they're related, but not interchangeable.

The student illustrates the first: our difficulty accepting independent chance. His "two bad lucks can’t happen in one day" resembles the gambler’s fallacy described in the heuristics-and-biases literature: the expectation that unfavorable outcomes should somehow balance themselves out over short stretches (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Chance has no memory; the exam and the lottery were never in conversation.

article continues after advertisement

The bridge between the gas station and what follows is unrealistic optimism. In classic studies, people systematically judged their own likelihood of negative life events—illness, accidents, addiction—as lower than that of comparable others (Weinstein, 1980). Knowing the population’s risk, it turns out, is one thing; believing oneself personally subject to it is another. I am different. The numbers describe other people. This is not arrogance; it is self-protection—acknowledging vulnerability would mean facing the anxiety we are trying to escape.

The husband shows the dangerous form of that exemption and one route people take to it: the illusion of control. His exercise reasoning was exactly this move. Langer (1975) showed that people can experience a sense of control even when outcomes are governed largely or entirely by chance. "I take care of my body, therefore I can control this risk" converts a general danger into a personally managed one. The exemption feels earned. It is not.

One further mechanism becomes relevant specifically in addiction: delay discounting, the tendency to value immediate rewards disproportionately over delayed consequences. A large meta-analysis found this tendency reliably steeper across addictive behaviors (MacKillop et al., 2011). The drink offers something now; many of its costs arrive later, and the ledger is settled against a future that may not honor the repayment plan.

The Recalculation That Never Came

Nearly two years passed. I thought little of either conversation until the wife walked into my office alone.

Her face told the story before she spoke. Her husband—the man who exercised daily, who was certain he had it under control—had died in a car accident. He had been driving drunk.

In that moment, the concepts I have just listed for you stopped being abstractions. They described some of the ways human beings can underestimate danger even while knowing, intellectually, that the danger exists. And now his wife was left to live with the consequences of a risk he had believed he could control.

The Only Honest Question

The student at the gas station was rehearsing the same script: The consequences apply to other people. He walked away that night having lost a few dollars. The husband drove away one night and never returned. The mechanisms differed in their details. The underlying move was the same: a known, general risk, personally waived. In one case, the error cost a few dollars. In the other, the consequences were irreversible.

article continues after advertisement

I once wrote that a car’s navigation system can teach us compassion: It never judges, it simply recalculates. But here is the hard companion truth. The road itself is not a GPS. Biology does not negotiate. Reality offers no unlimited recalculations—some wrong turns are final. Which means the recalculating must be done by us, and it must be done before the turn: at the store counter, before another pour, at the car keys, while the route can still be changed.

So the next time you catch yourself thinking that won’t happen to me, pause. Not because you are weak, but because you are human, and human beings are remarkably good at constructing reasons why a general risk may not apply to us personally. That student was not stupid. That husband was not a bad man. They were caught in the same seductive confusion: that awareness of risk is the same as immunity from it. It is not. Knowing the odds does not change them. Intention does not rewrite biology. And certainty does not stop a car.

The world will not recalculate for you.

You still can.

If you or someone you love is struggling with alcohol or substance use, confidential help is available: in the U.S., the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 (24/7); outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists local services.

item.title: Why Are Gifted Children, Teenagers, and Adults So Intense?
item.description:
Relationships

Why Are Gifted Children, Teenagers, and Adults So Intense?

How to react to the demanding, needy behavior of the gifted.

Posted August 8, 2026

Source: Pexels/Pixabay

Precocious children, with the help of their parents, relatives, teachers, and tutors, have to learn how to deal with the intellectual, emotional, and social challenges that extremely bright people struggle with on a day-to-day basis. As well, adults who are very bright need to understand how they are different from more “average” individuals. Are you wondering, “Why does understanding this issue help with high-strung children, teenagers, and adults?” Here are my answers.

1. Understanding gifted individuals’ intense questioning and almost desperate need for all kinds of challenges and attention is the most reasonable and effective way to deal with their endless interrogations. Being confrontational will not help. Avoid saying to your young child, “Information about space travel is for older people to understand.” Or, “Stop asking questions; you are wearing me out.”

For example, your 5-year-old asks, “How does a spaceship with an astronaut aboard manage to come down to earth when it leaves the moon?” Do space travelers just jump off the rocket ship?”

Do you say, “Of course not!” You say that special procedures and instruments are used when you travel so many miles away from home. I have heard physicists talking with the astronauts who report that returning to earth is very, very scary, no matter how much scientific reasoning and computation has gone into the event.

Children and teenagers with inquisitive minds and lots of curiosity are really not dead-set on driving you crazy and wearing you out. When gifted individuals see something or hear something that they want to understand, they expect and are determined to find an answer. “Why is that man sleeping in the street? Why is my mommy crying? Why is my father so upset about his car repair bill? We have an extra car in our garage to use.” The answers to these types of questions are complicated, and explanations can take time and a lot of effort.

Actually, extremely smart and passionate children and adults are remarkably imaginative and even astonishing problem solvers. I remember many conversations I had with my gifted clients and my own children. I am still impressed, inspired, educated, and entertained by these conversations. Having raised two very curious individuals, I know firsthand that gifted children are really real!

In other words, they have not been coached by their parents to ask complicated and very serious questions. Real concerns about right and wrong, and good and bad, are common questions for children to explore with their parents, relatives, and teachers. Gifted individuals long desperately for answers to their own personal questions. This need for understanding is not prevalent for more “average” children and adults.

The reaction of “listeners” is also remarkable. Mom says to her own mother: “Is this really happening? My daughter is only four years old and wants to learn how to read. The classroom teacher thinks I am just bragging when I am asking for the school’s help.” Grandma has lots of empathy for her daughter’s confusion about how to raise a gifted child.

2. Giftedness can be intimidating for an average person who has not had any experience with exceptionally smart and talented individuals. Again, the average person is puzzled by special abilities that are not seen on an everyday basis. Even if you are around gifted people, it is still incredible to watch their distinctive and quick talents and abilities.

article continues after advertisement

How do parents and teachers come to understand giftedness in a way that will help them support their children and develop their true identity?

Here are my suggestions:

1. Do your research: Knowledge that you acquire from books and interacting with other people goes a long way to understanding quick and emotional persons.

2. Seek help from professionals who work with gifted kids and adults.

3. Avoid talking behind people’s backs about their children, friends, or colleagues.

How to React to the Neediness of Gifted Individuals

1. React calmly with interest and sensitivity to their curiosity and need to be understood and helped.

2. Carefully listen to what they are asking for in terms of help and understanding.

3. Offer the support that you can give, even if you believe that they want more from you than you can give. Overdoing will always backfire on you.

Concluding Remarks

My best advice for dealing with giftedness is to acquire as much knowledge based on experience and actual observation as you can. While education and enthusiasm are important to the gifted child, too much is just too much. Try to teach your gifted kids to relate to others who may not be as smart as they are. My brother and his wife are scientific geniuses who cannot relate to the non-gifted world. It is sad to observe the awkwardness that emerges when gifted people are judging the non-gifted and non-gifted people (you could say average or normal) are judging them in turn. Try to be accepting of different abilities and appreciate the good in each person.

item.title: The Process and the Practice of Grief
item.description:
Grief

The Process and the Practice of Grief

Grief informs us of the value of something we have lost.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • We see the tragedy our clients experience but cannot be flooded by it, or we wouldn't be able to do our work.
  • Meaning-making is a stage of grief that helps us integrate grief into life purposefully.
  • Grief and depression may coincide but may be mutually exclusive; clinicians need to be sensitive to this.

Dr. Kübler-Ross, in her 1969 book, On Death and Dying, offered for the first time a framework for understanding grief, based on her research with terminal patients. Her model is not linear, and individuals may cycle through or revisit as needed.

Kübler-Ross, a psychiatrist, describes denial, the first stage of grief, as a defense mechanism where our minds numb us to the immediacy of the loss. The next stage is anger, where the denial gives way to feelings of anger at the pain experienced from the loss or at external circumstances brought about by the loss. The third stage is bargaining, where we might try to negotiate the pain of the loss away by perhaps imagining different outcomes. Then we may experience feelings of depression characterized by the weight of what has occurred, expressed with sadness, isolation, or hopelessness. The final stage is acceptance, which might be best described as learning to live with the permanent pain and changes it brings to how life was.

Dr. David Kessler, a grief expert, has added another stage he describes as meaning, which allows a person to move forward, honor the loss in some way, and find a way to integrate the experience into a purposeful life.

The DSM-5-TR pathologizes grief by calling it Prolonged Grief Disorder, and it adheres to a caveat of more days than not and over a month of intense yearning and preoccupation with thoughts or memories of the deceased person. A person must exhibit marked disbelief about death and avoidance of reminders of the deceased, and experience three symptoms from a laundry list that includes identity disturbance, reminders of loss, intense emotional pain, and more.

This historical development is presented as a long-term process culminating in the inclusion of valid, clinically relevant prolonged grief disorder criteria in diagnostic handbooks. Yet there are challenges to this dominant narrative. As stated in a 2023 article (Eisma, 2023): "[T]he developmental history of prolonged grief disorder has been nonlinear and...this yields questions on generalizability and problems with measurement.” Grief and depression may certainly coincide, but they also may be mutually exclusive, and we as clinicians need to be sensitive to this.

Grief may also tell us we lost something important that may not be a person, but something else. Grief informs us of the value of something we have received. As I work with individuals who suffer from severe and persistent mental illness, I witness loss often. The person who hears voices marching through their head or believes they are being followed may grieve the absence of quiet and safety.

Individuals who have been sexually or physically abused as children, those who lack loving and committed parents, homeless or hungry persons, or those who suffer from a pervasive life-changing mental illness grieve for those losses they have experienced, yet they don’t have the luxury to grieve because their lives are filled with instincts to survive.

article continues after advertisement

Illegal immigrants who live in fear of being deported at any moment cannot grieve their loss of hope about the lives they believed they would have had. It is ever-present grief about the immediacy of impending loss.

I believe grief also takes us to a darker side of life we would rather not see. For those of us in mental health care, we see the tragedy our clients have experienced routinely, but we cannot be flooded with grieving, or we would be unable to do our work.

Grief is a multidimensional experience that all of us will experience or have experienced in our lives. Perhaps it is the experience that has allowed us to go deeper inside ourselves to serve others. It is a common occurrence that we don’t speak enough about.

I had a client I worked with for 20 years. She suffered not only severe and persistent mental illness but also borderline personality disorder. I met her in a clinic I was working in and was able to accommodate her in my private practice following my leaving the clinic.

She was a unique human being, but she had spent her life cutting her arms and pushing people away and hearing voices when no one was around. She was a pacifist and often went to marches to proclaim nonviolence.

Over time, she abandoned her cutting behaviors in favor of developing relationships with others and expressing her deep feelings openly and with less fear and intensity. Her favorite method of being pampered was being psychiatrically hospitalized at a few chosen sites. Not only a particular hospital but a designated floor.

article continues after advertisement

When she was 51 years old, she was diagnosed with lung cancer. When oxygen became necessary, she could not visit my office, so I decided to have our sessions at her house.

She became less able to care for herself and did not have any care providers, so she moved into a nursing home where she would be able to be transported to a hospital for her chemotherapy and radiation. The rides became very painful. She needed to be wheeled into an ambulance and take the bumpy ride to treatment. After a few treatments, she elected to discontinue both. She was going to die.

I once again decided that I would conduct therapy where she was living, in a private room, which she was wheeled into. This continued for months as she weakened, but she was still committed to working in therapy.

This process forced me to consider the purpose of psychotherapy and the surroundings in which it occurs.

She had requested my attendance at her bedside as death approached. I remained one day when she passed. Having received verbal permission to speak at her funeral, I gave the eulogy.

My grief was not like it was for other deaths I had previously experienced. It was a deep-felt awareness of my connection to someone with whom I had passed through different stages of her life. I felt a gratitude, a joy, a sadness, and privilege to have known someone who changed my life and helped me become a deeper, more compassionate, more skilled practitioner. It was David Kessler’s stage of meaning.

Fifteen years later, her calligraphy hangs in my home, and her dream catcher hangs in a window.
